p: Ezekiel turns his face toward a target to speak against it.
b: The Hebrew is sim panim 'put the face', a prophet's act of aiming his gaze, and so his message, at a place or people. Ezekiel does it to the mountains of Israel (6:2), to Jerusalem (21:2), to Sidon (28:21), to Pharaoh (29:2), to Mount Seir (35:2) and to Gog (38:2). The gesture is always hostile here. Foreign nations were not present to hear it. The oracle was spoken or acted before the exiles, who are the real audience, and it worked on them as a promise that their neighbors would be judged.

p: Ammon lay east of the Jordan, around Rabbah, today's Amman.
b: The Ammonites lived on the plateau east of the Jordan, with their capital at Rabbah. They had been Israel's rivals since the days of Jephthah and Saul. In Ezekiel's time Ammon sent envoys to the meeting of small kings in Jerusalem about 594 BC (Jeremiah 27:3), raided Judah under Babylonian orders (2 Kings 24:2), and after the fall of Jerusalem its king Baalis sheltered Ishmael, who killed Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:14; 41:10). Ezekiel has two words against Ammon: this one, and the sword that Nebuchadnezzar points at Rabbah (Ezekiel 21:19-23, 28-32). Amos and Zephaniah also accuse Ammon (Amos 1:13-15; Zephaniah 2:8-11).
r: Jeremiah 27:3; Jeremiah 40:14; Jeremiah 49:1-6; 2 Kings 24:2; Amos 1:13-15; Zephaniah 2:8-11; Ezekiel 21:28-32

p: Ezekiel's usual way to open a word from God.
b: The Hebrew is koh amar Adonai YHWH, the messenger's formula 'Thus says the Lord GOD', which Ezekiel uses far more than any other prophet. 'The Lord GOD' (Adonai YHWH) is the site's rendering of the two names together: Adonai is 'the Lord' and YHWH, God's own name, is 'GOD' in capitals so that it is not mistaken for the title (elsewhere YHWH alone is 'the LORD'). Ezekiel writes it 217 times, 24 of them in these four chapters. The formula closes with ne'um Adonai YHWH, 'the Lord GOD declares', which is an 'utterance', a noun, not a verb.
orig: כֹּה־אָמַר אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (koh amar Adonai YHWH)

p: A cry of cruel delight at someone's disaster.
b: He'ach is a gloating cry. It is what the enemies of the psalmist shout when he falls (Psalm 35:21, 25; Psalm 40:15). Ammon, Tyre and the nations in general are charged with it when Jerusalem falls (Ezekiel 26:2; 36:2). The charge in each oracle is the same: they did not just watch. They celebrated, and treated the fall of God's sanctuary as their gain. Ezekiel names three things Ammon cheered at: the profaning of the Temple, the emptying of the land, and the exile of Judah.

p: Desert tribes who come in from the steppe and settle where a nation fell.
b: Bene qedem, 'sons of the east', are the nomadic and seminomadic peoples of the Syrian and Arabian steppe: Jacob goes to their land (Genesis 29:1), Midian and Amalek come with them as raiders in Gideon's day (Judges 6:3, 33), and Job is 'the greatest of all the people of the east' (Job 1:3). The oracle says that Ammon and Moab will be taken over by such people. The text does not name an empire or a date. It describes a slow takeover by herders who camp in the ruined towns. Later records show Arab tribes, and then the Nabateans, spreading across Transjordan.

a: Then you will know that I am the LORD
t: 'Then you will know that I am the LORD'
p: The line that closes most of Ezekiel's oracles, nine times in these four chapters.
b: This is the 'recognition formula', one of the marks of the book. In these four chapters it ends oracles at 25:5, 7, 11, 17; 26:6; and 28:22, 23, 24, 26. In 25:14 the object changes: 'they will know my vengeance'. In 28:24 it is 'I am the Lord GOD'. The point is that every judgment, on Israel or on its neighbors, is a lesson about who the LORD is. Even the nations' ruin is not about them alone. The Plain keeps one English sentence each time, because the repetition is the book's voice.
orig: וִידַעְתֶּם כִּי־אֲנִי יְהוָה (vida'tem ki ani YHWH)

a: all the scorn that was in you
p: The Hebrew puts 'scorn' with nefesh, the whole self, in 25:6 and 25:15.
b: The Hebrew joins 'scorn' to nefesh ('self', 'life', 'inner being', often 'soul') in 25:6 and again in 25:15. The Plain keeps 'heart' for lev and says 'that was in you' here and 'from deep inside' in 25:15, so that the two verses can be seen to use one word.

a: the same as all the nations
p: Moab says Judah's God has no special power; Ezekiel heard the same taunt from Israelites.
b: The sneer is that the house of Judah is nothing special, with a God who could not protect it. It sounds like the exiles' own words in Ezekiel 20:32: 'Let us be like the nations'. The charge is not mere cruelty. By denying that Judah is different, Moab denies that the LORD is different from Chemosh and the other gods. Compare Zephaniah 2:8-10, where Moab and Ammon are also charged with mocking God's people.

t: The three towns of Moab's northern edge
p: Moab's 'glory' was a string of towns on its northern frontier.
b: These three towns stood on the northern edge of Moab, facing the Jordan valley. Israel had once held them: Reuben rebuilt Kiriathaim and Baal-meon (Numbers 32:37-38), and Beth-jeshimoth was in the plains of Moab where Israel camped (Numbers 33:49). In the Mesha Stele of about 840 BC, the Moabite king boasts that he built Baal-meon and Kiriathaim after throwing off Israel. Ezekiel names them as the doors through which the people of the east will pour in. To 'open the flank' is to remove the defense on that side.

p: The Hebrew is clipped; it can mean 'as well as Ammon'.
b: The Hebrew says 'to the sons of the east, upon the sons of Ammon' (al bene Ammon). It may mean 'in addition to the Ammonites' (the people of the east are being given Ammon as well as Moab), which is how the Plain takes it, or 'together with the Ammonites'. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has the same clipped phrase, so it does not remove the puzzle. The sense for the oracle is clear either way: Ammon's name will not be remembered among the nations.

p: Edom's offence was joining in when Jerusalem fell.
b: Edom was Jacob's brother Esau, and the two peoples were bound by kinship and old quarrels (Genesis 25:30; 36:1). When Jerusalem fell, Edom is accused of standing aside, rejoicing and looting (Obadiah 10-14; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22). How much Edom actually did is debated: some scholars read Obadiah as exaggerated, others as accurate. In any case, Edom and the Philistines are both charged with vengeance, a word that sounds again and again through 25:12-17. A longer word against Mount Seir, which is Edom, comes in chapter 35.
r: Obadiah 10-14; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Jeremiah 49:7-22; Amos 1:11-12; Ezekiel 35:1-15

a: From Teman as far as Dedan
p: The line runs from Edom's heartland to an oasis far to the south.
b: Teman is the chief region of Edom (Jeremiah 49:7, 20; Amos 1:12; Obadiah 9). Dedan was an Arabian caravan oasis far to the southeast, usually placed at al-Ula in northwest Arabia. Ezekiel's Hebrew has the ending -ah on 'Dedan', which means 'toward', so the line reads 'from Teman, and toward Dedan, they will fall by the sword.' It can also be read as two places, Teman and Dedan, both falling. Genesis lists two Dedans, one a son of Raamah (Genesis 10:7) and one a son of Jokshan (Genesis 25:3); Ezekiel names Dedan again as a trader in 27:15, 20.

a: by the hand of my people Israel
p: Edom was later conquered by Judah's Maccabean rulers; Jewish writers then used 'Edom' for Rome.
b: The oracle gives Israel itself the task of judging Edom. Judah did take Edom's land at various times; Judas Maccabeus fought the sons of Esau (1 Maccabees 5:3), and John Hyrcanus forced the Idumeans, as Edom was then called, to be circumcised and live as Jews (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257-258). Whether that fulfils this oracle is a reading, not a given: Edom's decline came first under Babylon (Nabonidus is thought to have campaigned there) and then through the Nabateans, who moved into Edom's heartland. Later Jewish writing used 'Edom' as a code name for Rome, and so applied oracles like this one to Rome.

t: The Philistines and the end of their cities
p: Babylon destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BC; the Philistine cities never came back as nations.
b: The 'old hatred' goes back to Samson and Saul and David (Judges 13-16; 1 Samuel 4-7; 17). Judah's Philistine neighbors shared the Babylonian-era disaster: the Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in 604 BC and left it a ruin, and Jeremiah 47 speaks of the same period. After the exile the Philistines no longer appear as a people; the region's name 'Palestine' is Greek and Roman, from their name.

p: The Kerethites were part of the Philistine world and came from the Aegean.
b: The Kerethites are 'Cretans' in the Greek (Krêtas). They appear as part of the south coast of Canaan (1 Samuel 30:14; Zephaniah 2:5) and, with the Pelethites, as David's bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18). The Philistines themselves came from Caphtor, which is probably Crete or the Aegean (Amos 9:7; Jeremiah 47:4). The ancient pun is that 'cut off the Kerethites' (hikhrati et-kerethi) sounds like 'cut off the cut-off', since karat means 'cut'.

a: the first day of the month
p: The Hebrew gives the year and the day but not the month.
b: The Hebrew has 'in the eleventh year, on the first of the month'. The month name has dropped out in the Hebrew, and the Greek printed by Swete has the same gap. The eleventh year, counted from Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC, is 587/586 BC, the year Jerusalem fell (in the fourth month, Jeremiah 52:6). So the oracle falls close to the fall of the city, and Tyre's 'Aha!' in verse 2 assumes it has already fallen. But Ezekiel hears the news only in 33:21-22, a year later by the book's own dating. The eleventh year runs from spring 587 to spring 586 BC, so the date could fall before the fourth-month fall of the city as well as after it. Readers explain the "Aha!" by prophetic knowledge, by a later date for the news in chapter 33, or by taking verse 2 as a quotation of what Tyre would say.

a: The doors of the peoples are smashed
p: Jerusalem sat on the inland trade routes; with it gone, Tyre's trade could grow.
b: 'The doors of the peoples' is Jerusalem seen as a gate on the land routes between Egypt, Arabia and the north. Tyre was a sea trader, and Jerusalem's fall removed a rival and opened the caravan trade to Tyre ('it has turned to me'). Tyre's king had sent envoys to the meeting of small kings in Jerusalem about 594 BC (Jeremiah 27:3). He was no friend of Babylon, but he was ready to profit from Judah's loss. Joel 3:4-6 and Amos 1:9-10 charge Tyre with trading in captured people, which is the money that fills Tyre.

p: A formula of challenge, as if the LORD stepped into the ring.
b: Hinni alayikh is God's declaration of war on a named target. It appears against Jerusalem (Ezekiel 5:8), the false prophets (13:8), Sidon (28:22), Pharaoh (29:3), Mount Seir (35:3) and Gog (38:3), and in Nahum 2:13 against Nineveh and Jeremiah 50:31 against Babylon. It often comes first, before any reason or sentence. In Tyre's case it is followed at once by the sea image, which fits a city whose power was the sea.
r: Ezekiel 5:8; Ezekiel 28:22; Ezekiel 29:3; Ezekiel 38:3; Nahum 2:13; Jeremiah 50:31

a: the way the sea makes its waves rise
t: The sea turned against the sea city
p: Tyre's strength was the sea, so the attack comes as the sea.
b: The nations rise against Tyre as the sea rises with its waves. Tyre ruled the sea by its ships, and the image turns the sea's own power against it: ships and walls could not stop waves. Later verses carry the water through the whole oracle: the island is a place for nets (26:5), its stones are thrown into the water (26:12), the deep covers it (26:19), and the ship Tyre breaks in the heart of the seas (27:26-27). Compare Jeremiah 51:42, where the sea rises over Babylon.

p: A title of the great Mesopotamian kings, here given to Nebuchadnezzar.
b: Melekh melakhim is the Hebrew form of the Akkadian sharru sharrani, a title used by Assyrian and Babylonian rulers. Daniel 2:37 gives it to Nebuchadnezzar as well, and Ezra 7:12 to the Persian king. Ezekiel does not mean it as praise: this king is the LORD's tool, brought from the north by the LORD himself ('I am about to bring'). The title is later given to Christ (Revelation 19:16) and to God (1 Timothy 6:15), in another turn of the same language.

p: A thirteen-year siege, reported by Josephus from the Phoenician historian Menander.
b: Josephus, quoting the Phoenician historian Menander of Ephesus, says that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years in the reign of its king Ittobaal (Against Apion 1.156; compare Antiquities 10.228). Counted from the 580s, the siege ended about 573 BC. The result was not a sack. Ezekiel himself, in 29:17-20, says that Nebuchadnezzar and his army worked hard against Tyre and got no wages from it, and Tyre seems to have come to terms and accepted Babylonian rule, and the royal house changed (Menander names a king Baal next). Babylonian records of the siege itself are not known to survive.

p: Three Hebrew words for a siege wall, a ramp and a shield wall.
b: Dayeq is a siege wall or a ring of works built around the city (the same word as in 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4), solelah is a ramp of earth and timber piled up against the wall, and tsinnah is a large shield, so a 'wall of shields', either a screen of soldiers' shields or a movable cover for the attackers. Each is a standard element of the siege of a city on a hill. Tyre's island walls stood in the sea. Siege works like these suit the mainland city and its towns, while the island could be reached only by ships or a causeway; the oracle runs the two cities together.

p: The ram and the 'blades' are rare words; the sense is from context.
b: The Hebrew for 'battering ram' is qobol (the blow of his 'qobol'), which occurs only here and so is a guess from context. The word for the tools that break the towers, charavot, literally means 'swords' or 'blades'. Many translations say 'axes' or 'crowbars'. The Plain follows the Hebrew letters and says 'blades'. A siege of this kind used rams, picks and fire against a wall, and the exact device is less important than the picture of the walls coming down.

p: Tyre's temple was famous for its pillars; Hiram of Tyre also made two for Solomon.
b: Matstsevot are standing stones or pillars, and 'pillars of your strength' may point to the great pillars of the sanctuary of Melqart, Tyre's god. Herodotus saw the temple at Tyre and wrote of two pillars in it, one of gold and one of green stone that shone at night (Histories 2.44). The Tyrian craftsman Hiram made the two bronze pillars of Solomon's Temple, Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:13-22). The Hebrew could also mean 'the pillars of your fortification'. Either way, the pillars stand for the city's public, religious and political strength.

a: into the middle of the water
p: In 332 BC Alexander built a land bridge to Tyre from the old mainland city's rubble.
b: When Alexander the Great besieged island Tyre in 332 BC he built a causeway to it, using stone and timber from the abandoned mainland town (Curtius 4.2.18; Diodorus 17.40). Many readers see 26:4, 12 and 14 as a precise forecast of this. Others point out that the Hebrew verbs here are plural ('they'), after Nebuchadnezzar's 'he' in verses 7-11, and speak of 'many nations' (26:3), so that the picture is a sequence of invaders, with no single named fulfilment. That argument rests on the Hebrew alone: in Swete's Greek the verbs of 26:12 are singular ('he will plunder ... he will pull down'), as in 26:7-11. Critics add that Tyre was resettled and flourished, and Ezekiel himself admitted the Babylonian siege did not achieve what was said (29:18).

a: You will never be built again
p: Tyre was rebuilt. The readings differ on what the sentence meant.
b: Tyre did not stay in ruins: after Alexander it was rebuilt and was a leading port under the Seleucids and Rome, and Paul found disciples there (Acts 21:3-6). Four readings: (1) Literal and exact: the 'bare rock' was the mainland city, which was never rebuilt; some popular books, such as Stoner's Science Speaks, argue this. (2) The sentence is about Tyre's pride and its great power, which really did end. (3) Ezekiel's own later word in 29:17-20 shows that the earlier oracle was not a mechanical timetable; readers who hold this take the 'never built again' as the end of Tyre's power. (4) Critical scholars treat it as a prophecy that was partly not fulfilled.

p: The Hebrew 'iyyim names the coasts and islands that traded with Tyre.
b: The Hebrew is iyyim, the plural of i, 'coast' or 'island'. The site's term for it is 'islands', meaning the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean, and the Plain uses it here and in Ezekiel 26:18; 27:3, 6, 7, 15 and 35. The Plain of Isaiah 23:2 and 6 says 'coastland' for the same Hebrew word. The sense is one: the sea-facing lands and ports that lived by Tyre's trade.

p: The rulers of Tyre's colonies and trading partners go through mourning.
b: 'The princes of the sea' are the chiefs of the coastal cities and islands that traded with Tyre or that were its colonies or allies. They act out the standard stages of mourning: they come down from their thrones, take off their robes and sit on the ground in trembling (compare Jonah 3:6 and Job 2:13). The image is of a trading empire that collapses with its center, because its trading partners were also its allies.

p: A qinah is a funeral song, sung over someone who has died.
b: Qinah 'lament' names both a type of poem and its rhythm. A qinah has a limping meter, a long line followed by a shorter one (three beats, then two), as if the singer is catching his breath. David sang one over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17-27). Ezekiel is told to take up a qinah over Jerusalem's princes (19:1), over Tyre here and in 27:2, 32 and 28:12, and over Pharaoh (32:2, 16). A lament in the mouth of a prophet is ironic: it mourns a city the LORD himself brings down.
r: 2 Samuel 1:17-27; Ezekiel 19:1; Ezekiel 27:2; Ezekiel 28:12; Ezekiel 32:2; Amos 5:1-2

p: The Hebrew says 'inhabited from the seas'; the text may be damaged.
b: The Hebrew is noshevet miyyammim, literally 'inhabited from the seas'. The best sense is that Tyre was peopled by seafarers, or that its people came from across the seas. Some scholars think a letter has dropped and read 'you who sat on the seas'. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has 'How were you destroyed from the sea, praised city', with no 'inhabited'. The Plain keeps the Hebrew words as they stand.

p: The 'deep' (tehom) is the watery chaos of Genesis 1:2, now covering Tyre.
b: Tehom 'the deep' is the ocean of Genesis 1:2, the water that was there before creation and that God holds back. In the flood it rises (Genesis 7:11) and in Jonah it closes over the prophet (Jonah 2:5). Here it is sent against a city of the sea, and the picture is of creation being undone for Tyre. The related Babylonian word Tiamat is a goddess in the Babylonian creation story, but the Hebrew word is not a god, and the Bible uses it for a physical sea. The tie to Babylonian myth is a debated question.

t: The Pit and the people of long ago
p: Tyre goes down to the world of the dead among those who died long ago.
b: Bor 'pit' or 'cistern' is a word for the grave and for Sheol, the world of the dead (Isaiah 14:15; Psalm 28:1; Psalm 88:4). Ezekiel returns to it for Pharaoh and the nations in chapters 31 and 32. 'The people of long ago' (am olam) are the dead of ancient times, whose ruins lie under the earth. The contrast is with 'the land of the living', the world where the LORD will 'set splendor', that is, Jerusalem restored. Tyre goes down into the earth and Israel is raised.
r: Isaiah 14:15; Psalm 28:1; Psalm 88:4; Ezekiel 28:8; Ezekiel 31:14; Ezekiel 32:18

p: 'Perfect in beauty' is what Psalm 50 and Lamentations 2 call Zion.
b: Kelilat yofi 'complete in beauty' is a name of Zion. Lamentations 2:15 has passers-by ask whether this ruined city is the one called by exactly these words, and Psalm 50:2 says God shines out of Zion with a related phrase, mikhlal yofi. Ezekiel 16:14 says Jerusalem's beauty was complete because of the LORD's splendor. When Tyre calls itself kelilat yofi, it claims the title of the holy city. The same words return in 28:12, where the lament calls the king 'complete in beauty'.

p: Tyre had a harbor facing north (the Sidonian) and one facing south (the Egyptian).
b: Tyre sat at the 'entrances' of the sea: its island had a harbor on the north side, called the Sidonian harbor, and another on the south, called the Egyptian. Ancient sources describe the double harbor. Chapter 27 uses a shipbuilding poem to praise Tyre, then lists its trade partners. Many of the names, among them Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Togarmah, Dedan, Sheba, Raamah and Asshur, are also in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10, though not in its order. The Plain renders sochar 'trader' and rokhel 'dealer' throughout the list. Compare also the shorter list in Isaiah 23:1-3.

p: Each part of the ship comes from a famous source.
b: Every part comes from a different land: cypress from Senir (the Amorite name for Mount Hermon, Deuteronomy 3:9), cedar from Lebanon, oaks from Bashan, ivory and pine from Cyprus, linen from Egypt, purple dye from Elishah. The Hebrew berushim is a tree, probably cypress or juniper. The word for 'planks' is unusual. The list shows Tyre as a floating catalogue of the world's finest goods, with Tyre itself as the one who 'perfected' them.
r: Deuteronomy 3:9; Song of Songs 4:8; 1 Kings 5:8; Isaiah 2:13

t: A hard phrase for the deck
p: The Hebrew is 'ivory, daughter of Asshurim'; most read it as a kind of tree.
b: The Masoretic Text reads shen bat-ashurim, 'ivory, daughter of Asshurim'. Most commentators join the last words into one tree name, bat-te'ashshur, 'in boxwood' (compare Isaiah 41:19), and the Plain's 'pine' follows a guess for the same tree. Read as two words they mean 'daughter of Asshurim', which makes no clear sense. The sentence is a ship's deck of ivory inlaid in some fine wood, from the islands of Cyprus (Kittim).

p: The Phoenician cities supplied sailors, officers and repairers.
b: Sidon and Arvad (Arwad, an island city to the north) supplied Tyre's rowers, and Gebal (Byblos, 27:9) its caulkers. The city-states of the Phoenician coast acted as one fleet under Tyre. 'Pilots' translates chovlim, literally those who handle the ropes. The poem does not mean that Tyre had foreign slaves at the oars. It means that the whole coast worked for Tyre's trade and, in verses 10-11, its defense.

a: Men from Persia, Lud and Put
p: Tyre hired soldiers from Iran, Anatolia and Africa.
b: Persia (Paras) is the Iranian highlands. This is among the first times the name appears in the Bible; Ezekiel uses it again in 38:5, with Cush and Put. Lud is either Lydia in western Anatolia or an African people (Genesis 10:13, 22), and Put is Libya or the Horn of Africa (Genesis 10:6). They hung their shields on Tyre's walls, as decorations that also proclaimed Tyre's wealth. The same three names, with Cush, appear as Egypt's allies in Ezekiel 30:5.

p: An unknown word. Ancient translators guessed 'guards' and 'dwarfs'.
b: Gammadim occurs only here, and no people called this is known. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has 'guards' (phylakes) in the towers. Other guesses have ranged from a Syrian place name to a word for short men (from gomed, a short cubit), but nothing is certain. The Plain keeps the Hebrew name. In the same verse the word before 'on your walls' has the consonants of 'your army' (the Greek has 'your force'), but some translators take it as a place name, Helech. The Plain follows 'your army'.

p: Tarshish was a far western source of silver, iron, tin and lead.
b: Tarshish is a distant western place, usually identified with Tartessos in southern Spain, whose silver and tin supplied the Phoenicians (compare Jeremiah 10:9, 'silver from Tarshish'). Jonah tried to flee to Tarshish, as far from the LORD's call as a ship could go (Jonah 1:3). The Greek translates Tarshish as 'Carthaginians' (Karchedonioi), which is a translator's choice. 'Ships of Tarshish' became a phrase for large merchant ships, as in Isaiah 23:1 and Psalm 48:7.

p: Slaves are listed with bronze among Tyre's goods; Revelation 18 repeats the line.
b: The Hebrew is nefesh adam, 'the life of a human being', meaning slaves. Javan (Greece), Tubal and Meshech (Anatolia) supplied them, as they supplied bronze. The charge fits Joel 3:4-8, where Tyre and Sidon sold the people of Judah to the Greeks, and Amos 1:9-10, where Tyre handed over whole communities to Edom. Revelation 18:13 ends its list of Babylon's cargo with 'human souls', the same expression in the Greek of both books, in different cases (en psychais anthropon in Ezekiel, psychas anthropon in Revelation), and so tells readers that Babylon's wealth, like Tyre's, was built on the trade in human beings.

p: Togarmah lay in eastern Anatolia and was known for its horses.
b: Beth-togarmah, 'house of Togarmah', is a land in eastern Anatolia (the Hittite Tegarama), which supplied horses and mules. The Table of Nations makes Togarmah a son of Gomer (Genesis 10:3), and Ezekiel names it again among Gog's allies (38:6). The Hebrew parashim can mean 'horsemen' or a kind of horse, and the Plain says 'war horses'.

p: Pannag occurs once in the Bible; its meaning is unknown.
b: Judah and Israel supplied Tyre with food: wheat from Minnith (an Ammonite town, Judges 11:33), honey, oil and balm. The fourth word, pannag, occurs only here. Guesses include a sweet cake and millet; ancient translators were also guessing. Tyre depended on its neighbors' farms for food, as Acts 12:20 says again of Tyre and Sidon under Herod Agrippa, and Solomon had paid Hiram in wheat and oil (1 Kings 5:11).

t: Three names no one is sure of
p: The names in this verse are uncertain, and the Greek lacks 'Vedan'.
b: 'Vedan' (Vedan) may be 'and Dan', a place in Arabia, a slip for Dedan, or, with a small change, 'wine' (yayin) from Uzal. 'Javan' here is probably a different Javan than in verse 13, a place in Arabia. Uzal is a name in the list of Joktan's descendants in Genesis 10:27, and an old Arabic place name has been linked to it; this is uncertain. The Greek has 'from Asel' (ex Asel) and no Vedan.

p: Kedar was an Arab tribe that traded in sheep and goats.
b: Kedar, a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), was a confederation of tribes in the north Arabian desert, famous for black tents and flocks (Song of Songs 1:5; Isaiah 21:16-17; Jeremiah 49:28-29). Assyrian records name Qedar and its rulers. Here they bring animals for Tyre's use and for export. Sheep and goats were Tyre's meat, and wool its textile base.

t: This Eden is a place in Syria
p: Not the garden: Beth-eden is a north Syrian kingdom.
b: Haran, Canneh and Eden are towns or lands in Mesopotamia and Syria. 'Eden' here is Beth-eden or Bit-Adini, an Aramean kingdom on the Euphrates (Amos 1:5; 2 Kings 19:12: 'the people of Eden in Telassar'). It is spelled the same way as the garden's name in 28:13, but it is not the garden; readers should not carry the one into the other.

p: Several words are unclear; the Plain gives the likeliest sense.
b: This verse has words found nowhere else or rarely: makhlulim (splendid clothes), gelomim (cloaks), genazim (probably 'chests' or 'bundles'), chavushim ('bound'), arazim ('cedars', so cedar-wood chests or firmly made), and marketet (marketplace). The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has 'bringing blue and choice treasures bound with ropes, and things of cypress', which also suggests bundles and wooden goods. The picture is of a bazaar where cloth and wooden chests were traded. The Plain reads 'bales of many-colored cloth, tied with cords, and cedar chests'.

p: 'Heavy' and 'glorious' are the same Hebrew word.
b: Vatikhbedi comes from kaved, 'be heavy', which also means 'be honored' (the noun kavod is 'glory'). Tyre is both weighed down with cargo and honored for it. Isaiah 23:8 uses the same root of Tyre's merchants (nikbaddei erets, 'the honored of the earth'); the site's Isaiah Plain renders it 'the great names of the world'. The picture of a ship so full that it rides low becomes, in verse 26, a ship that sinks under its own load.

p: In Psalm 48:7 the east wind shatters 'ships of Tarshish'.
b: In the Mediterranean a strong east wind from the desert is dangerous to ships off this coast. The LORD uses it to break his enemies (Psalm 48:7: 'you shatter the ships of Tarshish with an east wind') and to dry up the vine of Judah (Ezekiel 17:10). The Greek printed by Swete has 'the south wind' instead (pneuma tou notou). In both readings the point is that the wind is the LORD's.

p: The sailors mourn in the standard ways; Israel itself was told not to shave for the dead.
b: Dust on the head, rolling in ashes, shaved heads and sackcloth are the marks of grief in many places (Job 2:12; Micah 1:10; Jeremiah 6:26). The sailors shave their heads, though Israel's law forbade this mourning custom (Deuteronomy 14:1; compare Leviticus 21:5). The point is that grief for Tyre will be shown in the manner of foreigners, and as wide as the sea. Revelation 18:19 has the shipmasters throw dust on their heads when Babylon falls.

a: you made the kings of the earth rich
p: Revelation 18 borrows this chapter's merchants, ships and mourners for Babylon.
b: Revelation's lament over Babylon borrows heavily from Ezekiel 27 without copying it line for line: the merchants and their cargoes (Revelation 18:11-13; Ezekiel 27:12-24), 'the kings of the earth' who grew rich on her trade (Revelation 18:3, 9; Ezekiel 27:33), the shipmasters who stand at a distance (Revelation 18:17-18; Ezekiel 27:29-30), the dust thrown on heads (Revelation 18:19; Ezekiel 27:30) and the question, 'Who was ever like Tyre?' (Revelation 18:18; Ezekiel 27:32). Revelation also uses Isaiah 23 and Jeremiah 51. Tyre becomes the pattern for the proud commercial empire.

p: The same word closes the oracles on Tyre in 26:21, 27:36 and 28:19.
b: Ballahot (plural of ballahah) comes from bahal, 'be terrified', and means a terror or a dreadful end. It marks the end of each of Ezekiel's three speeches on Tyre (26:21; 27:36; 28:19), with a matching close, 'you will be no more'. The same ending on all three makes the chapters one set. It occurs in Job 18:11, 14 and Psalm 73:19 for the sudden fall of the wicked.

p: Verses 1-10 speak to a 'ruler'; verses 11-19 to a 'king'.
b: The first speech is to the nagid of Tyre and the second to the melekh of Tyre. The Plain keeps the two titles apart: 'ruler', the site's rendering of nagid for a leader chosen or set by God (Saul and David are called this in 1 Samuel 9:16), and 'king'. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) calls both archon, 'ruler'. Josephus, quoting Menander, names Ittobaal as king of Tyre during Nebuchadnezzar's siege (Against Apion 1.156), and most commentators think he is the man addressed. Whether the 'ruler' and the 'king' are one person or the speeches differ in aim is debated; see 28:12.

p: Isaiah 14, Daniel 11 and Acts 12 tell the same story of a ruler who claims to be a god.
b: The ruler's boast has close relatives. The king of Babylon says, "I will make myself the Most High's equal." (Isaiah 14:14). The king of the north in Daniel exalts himself above every god (Daniel 11:36-37), and Paul's 'man of lawlessness' takes his seat in God's temple and declares that he is God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). In Acts 12:20-23 a delegation from Tyre and Sidon seeks Herod Agrippa's favor, the crowd at Caesarea shouts, "It's a god speaking, not a man!" (Acts 12:22), and he is struck down. The common thread is a human who forgets he is human, in the very words of Ezekiel's accusation: you are a human being and not a god.

t: The island as the gods' seat
p: Tyre's island was seen as a divine home in the middle of the sea.
b: Moshav elohim 'seat of gods' fits an island city whose patron god, Melqart, was believed to live there. Ancient Near Eastern texts speak of a divine home 'in the heart' of the waters: in the Ugaritic texts the high god El lives at the sources of the rivers, in the middle of the springs of the deep. Richard Clifford has set this and other 'cosmic mountain' ideas beside Ezekiel 28. The king claims the god's seat for himself; the LORD answers with the plain word 'human being' (adam), which is the word for the first man too. Rashi (on Sefaria) reads 'the seat of God' as a heaven-like structure the king built over the sea, a mechanism that imitated seven heavens, with himself on the highest.

p: This Daniel is a legendary wise man, spelled without a yod: DN'L. The Hebrew line is a taunt.
b: The Hebrew spells the name dn'l, as in Ezekiel 14:14, 20, and not the longer spelling of the book of Daniel. Two candidates: the Judean exile Daniel, taken to Babylon in 605 BC, famed for knowing secrets (Daniel 2); or Danel, a righteous king and judge in the Ugaritic story of Aqhat, an old tale known to Canaanites long before Ezekiel. John Day has argued for the Ugaritic figure in an article of 1980. The verse begins hinneh, 'look', and has no question word, so it can be read as a plain statement, a question or a sneer. Rashi, on Sefaria, reads it through Nebuchadnezzar's treatment of Daniel (Daniel 2:46) and calls both lines taunts. The Plain prints a sneer, with 'Look' and exclamation marks. Swete's Greek (Codex Vaticanus) makes both lines questions, and its second line differs from the Hebrew: 'You are not wiser than Daniel, are you? Did wise men not train you in their knowledge?' (mē sophoteros ei sy tou Daniel; sophoi ouk epaideusan se tē epistēmē autōn;), where the Hebrew has 'no secret is dark to you'.

p: The same words appear in verses 2, 5 and 17, tying the two speeches together.
b: Gavah libbekha, 'your heart has grown high', occurs in verse 2, verse 5 (over wealth) and verse 17 (over beauty). It is the sentence that ties the ruler of 28:1-10 to the king of 28:11-19. The same phrase describes Uzziah, whose strength made him proud (2 Chronicles 26:16), and Deuteronomy 8:14 warns Israel against a 'lifted' heart when it grows rich. The theme is the same whether the speech is about a ruler, a king or a fallen creature: success turns the heart upward.

p: Zarim are outsiders; here they are the foreign army.
b: The site renders zar 'outsider', someone who does not belong to a group. In the priestly laws it is a layperson (Exodus 29:33); in the prophets it is often a foreign enemy (Isaiah 1:7; Ezekiel 7:21; 11:9; 30:12). The same enemy is meant in verse 10. These 'outsiders' are Babylonians, and 'the most violent of the nations' fits Habakkuk 1:6-7 and Ezekiel 30:11; 31:12; 32:12.

p: In Ezekiel this means those outside Israel, who die without honor.
b: Arelim are the uncircumcised, here a label for outsiders who die without burial honors and without a place with their kin. Ezekiel 32:17-32 uses it again and again of the dead in Sheol: Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and Sidon lie there as 'the uncircumcised'. The sting is that the proud king of a rich city ends among the unnamed. Circumcision was not unique to Israel, since Egypt practiced it, so the word is not an ethnic tag but a statement of status in the world of the dead.

a: raise a lament over the king of Tyre
t: Who is the king of Tyre? Four readings
p: A human king in Eden's colors; Adam; Satan; or a retold myth. The chapter page sets out each.
b: (1) A human king of Tyre in Eden's colors: Zimmerli, Greenberg and Block, each in the volume listed. Rashi (Sefaria) takes him as a historical ruler; Radak, quoting the Targum, takes Eden as a figure for luxury. (2) The first man, Adam, as the pattern: Habel, in the article listed. (A rabbinic list, Derekh Eretz Zuta 1, counts Hiram of Tyre among nine who entered Eden alive; that is a legend about Hiram, not a reading of Ezekiel 28.) (3) A being behind the king, the rebel angel or Satan: Tertullian, Origen, Gregory the Great (nine stones, nine orders of angels, Homily 34 on the Gospels) and, much later, the Scofield Reference Bible. (4) An older Near Eastern myth of a primal figure on the mountain of God: Clifford (listed at 28:2) and those who follow him. Swete's Greek calls him archon 'ruler', as in 28:2, and makes the cherub a separate being (28:14, 16). No church builds its teaching on the fall of the angels on this passage; the chapter page says why there is no 'Where Christians differ' card.

a: set the seal on the pattern
p: The Hebrew is hotem tokhnit. Each word has more than one meaning.
b: The Masoretic Text points hotem as a participle, 'one who seals' (the KJV has 'thou sealest up the sum'), and the Plain follows it: 'one who set the seal on the pattern'. Rashi, on Sefaria, reads it so, as skill to stamp and seal every design. With other vowels the word is hotam, 'a seal', the noun the Greek reads (aposphragisma homoioseos, 'a seal of likeness'). Tokhnit means a measure, proportion or pattern (it is used of the Temple's design in Ezekiel 43:10). So the phrase may mean 'one who sets his seal on the finished pattern', 'a seal of perfect proportion' or 'a model of completeness'. All say that the king stood at the top of a well-made order.

a: In Eden, the garden of God, you were
p: Ezekiel's Eden has gems, a mountain and a cherub; Genesis 2-3 has gold and onyx but no such king.
b: Ezekiel calls the garden 'Eden, the garden of God' (gan-elohim; Genesis 13:10 has 'the garden of the LORD'). In Genesis the garden holds trees, a river and, at the east gate, cherubim after the expulsion (Genesis 3:24). Ezekiel's version has precious stones, the holy mountain of God, a cherub, and a figure who was 'created' blameless and later expelled. It is closer to Genesis than to any other text we have, but not the same story: there is no woman, no serpent and no forbidden tree. Scholars read this as another form of the Eden tradition, as Ezekiel's own reshaping of Genesis, or as a Tyrian tradition he turned against the king. Ezekiel uses Eden again for the trees of Assyria and Egypt in chapter 31. Genesis 2:11-12 does name gold and onyx (shoham) in the land of Havilah, two items that return in Ezekiel's list. The Greek (Swete) reads 'Eden' as a word, 'in the delight (tryphe) of the garden of God'.
r: Genesis 2:8-17; Genesis 3:24; Ezekiel 31:8-9; Ezekiel 31:16-18; Ezekiel 36:35; Isaiah 51:3

p: Hebrew nine stones; Greek twelve, like the high priest's breastplate.
b: The Plain gives the nine stones of the Hebrew list in the site's names for the same Hebrew words in Exodus 28:17-20: carnelian, topaz, quartz, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, lapis lazuli, turquoise and emerald. Their identification is uncertain (see the topic on precious stones). They are exactly the stones of the high priest's breastpiece (four rows of three) minus its third row, which the site's Exodus names jacinth, agate and amethyst. The Hebrew groups its nine in threes (an 'and' before every third name), but not in the order of the rows in Exodus. The Greek (Swete) has twelve names, in the order of the Greek of Exodus 28:17-20, with silver and gold added: sardion, topazion, smaragdos; anthrax, sapphire, iaspis; ligyrion, achates, amethystos; chrysolithos, beryllion, onychion. The three the Hebrew lacks are exactly the third row, which is the strongest sign that the Greek filled the list out to match Exodus. The Greek also leaves out 'the work of your tambourines and settings'. Revelation 21:19-20 has twelve foundation stones. Gregory the Great, in his Homily 34 on the Gospels, sets the nine stones of this verse beside the nine orders of angels, so for the Western reading it matters that the Hebrew has nine.

p: Toppekha and neqavekha are rare and could be instruments or jewelry settings.
b: Toph is a hand drum or tambourine (Exodus 15:20), and neqev is a hole or socket; in the plural it may mean 'pipes'. In a jewel context the pair is taken as 'settings and mountings' (the sockets in which stones are set), which is the standard modern reading. Radak, in the Sefaria text, reads them as musical instruments, 'drums and pipes'. The Plain keeps the literal words, because the Hebrew allows either: a king crowned with music, or one mounted in gold.

p: The Hebrew mimshach can mean 'anointed' or 'outstretched'; the Greek has 'with the cherub'.
b: The Hebrew is att-kerub mimshach hassokhekh: 'you, a cherub, [mimshach], the one who covers'. The Leningrad vowels give att, the feminine form of 'you' (the masculine is atta), which is one reason many scholars read the consonants as et, 'with', as the Greek does. Mimshach can come from mashach 'anoint' (so 'anointed') or from a root meaning 'stretch out'; the Latin Vulgate has extentus, 'stretched out'. Rashi (Sefaria) reads it as 'greatness': the cherub is a huge bird whose wings cover a wide dominion. The Plain says 'outspread' and adds no wings of its own; the wings are in the next word, 'the one who covers', which recalls the cherubim whose wings cover the ark (Exodus 25:20; 1 Kings 8:7).

p: Zion is called God's mountain; Isaiah 14 puts the proud king on a mountain too.
b: 'The holy mountain of God' (har qodesh elohim) is a cosmic mountain, the place where heaven and earth meet. In Israel it is Sinai (Exodus 3:1), then Zion (Psalm 48:1-2; Isaiah 2:2-3). Isaiah 14:13 has the king of Babylon say he will sit on 'the Mount of Meeting' in the far north (Zaphon), the mountain of the Canaanite storm-god Baal. Clifford argues that Ezekiel 28 draws on a Syro-Canaanite picture of the mountain where the high god had his garden. The king of Tyre is set there first and thrown from it later.

p: A phrase found only here: gems that flash, or the fiery stones of God's throne.
b: Avnei esh occurs only in 28:14, 16. It may mean flashing gems, like the gems that cover the king, or the glowing stones near God's throne, since Ezekiel's own vision of the throne has fire and gleaming stone (Ezekiel 1:13, 26-27; 10:2, 6). The line also recalls the 'sapphire pavement' under God's feet (Exodus 24:10). The sense is that the mountain of God is blazing with light.

p: Tamim: whole, with no flaw.
b: Tamim describes an animal fit for sacrifice, and a person who is whole in conduct (Noah, Genesis 6:9). The Plain says the king's ways were 'blameless', the site's rendering of tamim for a person. It says nothing about moral perfection in the later, absolute sense. The next lines say how the flaw came in: wrongdoing (avlah, 'crookedness' or 'injustice') was found in him, and his trading made it worse. The same root of 'wrong' is used for the dishonest scales of trade in Leviticus 19:35 and Ezekiel 3:20.

p: The sin named is violence done through trade, not rebellion in heaven.
b: The reason given for the fall is chamas, violence, which fills the king's 'midst' through his trading. In Ezekiel's world, Tyre's trade included the sale of people (27:13), which Joel 3:4-8 and Amos 1:9-10 call a crime. Chamas is also the reason for the flood (Genesis 6:11) and for the fall of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 7:11, 23; 8:17). Those who read the speech as the story of a human king point to this; those who read it of Satan find in 'you sinned' and 'wrong was found in you' a first sin of some being. The words are the same in both readings. In the Hebrew, 'I profaned you from the mountain of God' uses min ('from') for removal; the Plain keeps the words, and the sense is that God removed him.

a: To the ground I threw you
p: Isaiah 14:12 says 'hacked down to the ground'; Luke 10:18 and Revelation 12:9 use the picture of a fall.
b: The king is thrown 'to the ground' and exposed 'in front of kings' as a spectacle. Isaiah 14:12 has the Babylonian king 'hacked down to the ground' and 'fallen from the heavens'. Luke 10:18 has Jesus say he saw Satan fall like lightning, and Revelation 12:9 says the dragon was thrown down to the earth. Whether Ezekiel 28 is a source for these New Testament lines, or only a parallel, is the heart of the debate in the chapter page. The verb here is hishlakhtikha, 'I threw you'; the king's fall is God's act.

p: The word is plural: Tyre's temples, or the king's own holy places.
b: Miqdashekha 'your sanctuaries' is plural; the Greek (Swete) also has a plural (ta hiera sou) but turns the verb into God's own act: ebebelosa, 'I profaned your sanctuaries'. The Plain follows the Hebrew. It can mean the temples of Tyre, such as the temple of Melqart, or all the holy places that a king as priest-king was responsible for. The king did not defile the LORD's Temple; he defiled his own, by trade and by wrong. The last stage of the fall: fire comes 'from inside you', as in 19:14, where a fire from the vine's own branch consumes it.

p: In the Hebrew, 'profane' is said three times, with three different subjects: outsiders, God and the king.
b: The verb chalal 'profane' occurs three times in the two speeches, and in the Hebrew each time a different actor is the subject. Outsiders profane the king's splendor (28:7). God profanes the king (28:16, 'I profaned you'). The king profanes his own sanctuaries (28:18, 'you profaned'). So the fall has a human cause, a divine cause and a moral cause, and none cancels the others; giving divine and human causes together is a familiar feature of Ezekiel's judgments. The Greek (Swete) changes the third: it has 'I profaned your sanctuaries', so God is the subject twice and the king never. A second Hebrew verb of the same shape, chalal 'pierce', is behind 'those who pierce you' (28:9, mecholelekha), and the Greek of 28:16, 'you were wounded' (etraumatisthes), may have read that verb; the Plain's 'pierce' at 28:9 therefore hides a play on the sound of 'profane'.

p: Sidon is the only nation here with no reason given for its judgment.
b: Of the seven nations Ezekiel addresses, only Sidon has no stated charge. Instead the reason is in the next lines: its fall will clear 'stabbing briars' from Israel's side. Sidon, north of Tyre, was an older and sometimes greater Phoenician city (Isaiah 23:2, 4, 12). It joined the 594 BC meeting (Jeremiah 27:3). The Persian king Artaxerxes III crushed a Sidonian revolt about 345 BC and the city was burned (Diodorus 16.41-45).

p: In Ezekiel, God shows his holiness by acting in the sight of the nations.
b: 'Show myself holy' (niqdashti) is a key verb in Ezekiel. God's holiness is shown in judgment (here), in the gathering of Israel (28:25), and above all in the vindication of his name before the nations (20:41; 36:23; 38:16, 23; 39:27). The verb 'win glory' just before it (nikbadti) uses the same family as 'glory' (kavod). The pair appears in Leviticus 10:3, where God says he will show himself holy in those who come near him and gain glory in the sight of all the people.

p: A picture from the conquest, now turned around: neighbors are no longer thorns.
b: Thorn pictures for hostile neighbors go back to the conquest: if Israel did not drive the peoples out, they would be thorns in Israel's sides (Numbers 33:55; Joshua 23:13; Judges 2:3). Ezekiel himself was told that he lived among briars and thorns (2:6). The promise reverses this. The neighbors of Israel in the previous verses and in chapter 25, Tyre and Sidon, Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia, are the thorns, and their judgment is the removal of the thorns. Egypt follows in chapters 29-32.

p: A rarer form of the recognition formula, found here and in 13:9; 23:49; 24:24; 29:16.
b: Almost always the formula is 'you will know that I am the LORD'. In a few places it is 'I am the Lord GOD': here, and in Ezekiel 13:9; 23:49; 24:24; 29:16. These places follow a speech about Israel's own sin or its neighbors, so the form may belong to a group of passages that deal with Israel's relation to its neighbors. The difference is small, but the Plain keeps it.

p: The promise returns to Jacob's land, with Deuteronomy's gathering and Jeremiah's houses and vineyards.
b: The land was promised to Jacob (Genesis 28:13; 35:12). Ezekiel repeats the phrase 'my servant Jacob' in 37:25. The gathering 'from the peoples' recalls Deuteronomy 30:3-5. The picture of building houses and planting vineyards matches Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29:5) and the promise of Isaiah 65:21. 'Servant' (eved) here is a title of honor given to an ancestor, as to Abraham (Genesis 26:24), Moses and David. The chapter ends on the safe settlement: the section on the nations is for Israel's sake.
r: Genesis 28:13; Genesis 35:12; Deuteronomy 30:3-5; Jeremiah 29:5; Ezekiel 37:25; Isaiah 65:21
